title: Why blue is hard to find
body: Few plants and animals make a true blue pigment. Many natural blues, such as butterfly wings and bird feathers, are structural colour: tiny structures scatter or interfere with light so blue wavelengths reach your eye.

title: Why the sky is blue
body: Sunlight contains all colours. Air molecules scatter shorter, bluer wavelengths much more strongly than red ones (Rayleigh scattering), so blue light reaches you from every direction of the sky.
sourceTitle: NASA Space Place: Why Is the Sky Blue?

title: Why sunsets turn red
body: Near sunrise and sunset, light crosses much more atmosphere to reach you. Most blue light is scattered away along the path, so the reds and oranges are what remain.
sourceTitle: NOAA National Weather Service: Why is the sky blue?

title: Why leaves are green
body: Chlorophyll absorbs mostly red and blue light for photosynthesis and reflects much of the green, which is why healthy leaves look green.

title: Where autumn colours come from
body: As chlorophyll breaks down in autumn, yellow and orange carotenoids that were already in the leaf become visible. Many reds come from anthocyanins that some trees produce in autumn.
sourceTitle: Autumn leaf color (Wikipedia, with primary references)

title: Spirals in seed heads
body: Many plants place seeds or leaves about 137.5 degrees apart, which produces spiral counts that are often consecutive Fibonacci numbers. A large citizen-science study of sunflowers found that a notable share of heads did not follow the pattern.
sourceTitle: Swinton et al. 2016, Royal Society Open Science (PMC)

title: The nautilus is not golden
body: The chambered nautilus shell is a logarithmic spiral, but measurements show it is not the golden-ratio spiral it is often said to be.
sourceTitle: Golden ratio — disputed observations (Wikipedia, with primary references)

title: The rule of thirds is a habit, not a law
body: The rule of thirds is a composition guideline named by John Thomas Smith in 1797. It is a useful starting point for framing a scene, not a law of nature.

title: Why bees build hexagons
body: A grid of regular hexagons divides a flat surface into equal areas with the least total perimeter. This is the honeycomb conjecture, proved by Thomas Hales in 1999.
